title: Full Workshop: Build Your Own Deep Research Agents - Louis-François Bouchard, Paul Iusztin, Samridhi
talk_summary: A workshop from Towards AI building a deep-research agent (MCP server + Claude Code harness) feeding a deterministic writing workflow with an evaluator-optimizer loop, plus observability and LLM-judge evals. The most transferable parts are the split between flexible agentic research and constrained deterministic writing, structured-output reviews with priority ordering, and calibrating an LLM judge against a labeled dataset with F1 on dev/test splits.

takeaways.technique: Split exploratory agent from deterministic workflow, no orchestration
takeaways.what_they_do: They deliberately split the system into an agentic research stage (needs flexibility, pivoting, gap-filling) and a deterministic writing stage (needs constraint, tone, structure), and run them sequentially via a plain script sharing files rather than an orchestration framework.

takeaways.technique: Evaluator-optimizer with separate context window and structured reviews
takeaways.what_they_do: Writer produces a draft; a reviewer in a completely separate context window checks it against guideline, research, and profiles, and returns a list of Pydantic objects (profile, location, comment) so the editor knows exactly what was violated; loop runs a fixed number of iterations.

Because reviewers (human and LLM) comment on everything and reviews clash, they assign explicit priority: guideline/user intent first, then research (anti-hallucination), then style profiles, so the editor knows which to apply when findings conflict.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's super important to put a priority on them ... prioritize the guideline first, which is the user input, then the research, and then the profile

takeaways.technique: Calibrate LLM judge against labeled dataset with F1 on dev/test
takeaways.what_they_do: Build a dataset from real system outputs (never LLM-generated outputs), label pass/fail plus 2-3 sentence critique, split train/dev/test, use train as few-shot for the judge, tune on dev F1, validate on test F1, and watch for dev/test divergence as overfit signal.
takeaways.numbers: 20 real posts; 5 samples per split in demo; recommends 100+ for real use

takeaways.technique: Skills with progressive disclosure over always-loaded prompts
takeaways.what_they_do: They move long workflow instructions out of the always-present MCP prompt into a skill file; only name+description load until the skill is invoked, then the body loads and is wiped after the query, keeping the context lean.

takeaways.technique: MCP server for distributable business logic, skills for personalization
takeaways.what_they_do: They package tools/logic as an MCP server (dependencies, credentials, code encapsulated) so it can be shared across harnesses, and use skills only as the thin personalization layer on top; they also write every tool result to a .memory folder for logging and verification.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you want to distribute business logic, you don't really want to ask someone, 'Hey, download those skills, install these UV dependencies'
